lesson.title: Unpacking a List into Named Variables
lesson.summary: List unpacking assigns each element of a list to its own named variable in a single statement, and the star operator can collect any number of leftover elements into one list.
lesson.body:
You already know multiple assignment, writing something like x, y = 3, 7 to give two variables their values in one line. List unpacking is the same idea applied to a list that already exists: if the number of variables on the left matches the number of elements in the list on the right, Python assigns each element to the matching variable, in order.

```python
point = [3, 7]
x, y = point
print(x, y)
```

This prints:

```
3 7
```

Under the hood this is exactly the same mechanism enumerate() relies on when a for loop unpacks each index, value pair into two variables. The count has to match exactly, though: if point had three elements and you only wrote x, y = point, Python would raise a ValueError rather than silently dropping the extra value, because unpacking is meant to be exact and predictable, not forgiving.

Sometimes you know you want the first item, the last item, and everything in between as its own group, without knowing in advance how many middle items there are. The star operator, written before a variable name, tells Python to collect however many elements are left over into a list of their own.

```python
scores = [100, 85, 90, 77, 60]
first, *middle, last = scores
print(first)
print(middle)
print(last)
```

This prints:

```
100
[85, 90, 77]
60
```

first takes the very first element and last takes the very last one, exactly one value each, and *middle scoops up every element in between into a genuine list, [85, 90, 77], not just a reference to a slice of scores. Only one starred variable is allowed per unpacking statement, since Python needs to know unambiguously where the fixed variables end and the collected group begins. List unpacking is especially handy once a list's elements have a known meaning by position, such as a coordinate pair or a record with a clear first and last field, because naming each piece makes the code that follows far easier to read than repeatedly indexing into the original list.
